summary:
Sandhya Subramani demonstrates Scout, a four-legged rover built on a Raspberry Pi and connected over 4G from New York. She shows the robot obeying natural-language commands such as turning on headlights, greeting the audience, spinning 360 degrees, and answering a question it was never trained on—counting people visible in its front camera.

The technical core is an agentic layer built with Strands Agents, an open-source AWS framework. Traditional robots execute a fixed list of policies, but adding an LLM/agent layer lets the agent orchestrate which preset policy to call. Setup takes about five lines of code: import Strands, register the robot as a tool, and issue a natural-language command. Under the hood Strands uses Anthropic Claude Opus 4.8 as the model and OpenAI Realtime for voice.

Scout runs three simultaneous Strands agents: a thinker agent that continuously assesses the environment, a communication agent interfacing with Telegram and a web app, and a voice agent she disabled to avoid stage interruptions. The architecture has four layers—agent, policy provider, backend (simulation or hardware chip), and physical robot—with actions flowing down and observations flowing up. Strands supports 40+ robots across eight categories. Deployment is hybrid: VLA training happens in the cloud while execution can happen on the edge for speed. Strands decides which part to invoke, and safety guardrails are added.

In a closing Telegram demo she asks Scout to spin, analyze the room, and judge who is the best-looking person. Scout spins, scans with its camera, and picks the speaker—humorously noting her khaki jeans, sneakers, and confident stride against the blue curtain backdrop. She closes by noting Scout will always pick her as the prettiest.

sections.title: Meet Scout: Raspberry Pi + 4G rover
sections.summary: Sandy introduces Scout as her friendly rover and shows a screen capture of its view. She explains Scout runs on a Raspberry Pi in New York connected via SIM card and 4G.

sections.title: Natural-language commands and untrained counting
sections.summary: She demonstrates Scout turning on headlights, greeting the audience, spinning 360, and counting two people from its front camera despite never being trained to count people.

sections.title: Strands Agents: adding a brain to a robot
sections.summary: She introduces the open-source AWS Strands Agents framework, explains how an agent layer orchestrates which preset policy to invoke, and shows that wiring a robot to an agent takes about five lines of code.

sections.title: Three parallel agents on one robot
sections.summary: She explains Scout runs three Strands agents simultaneously: a thinker agent assessing the environment, a communication agent interfacing via Telegram and a web app, and a voice agent she disabled to stop on-stage interruptions.

sections.title: Four-layer architecture
sections.summary: She describes the four layers—agent, policy provider, backend (simulation or hardware chip), and physical robot—where instructions flow down and observations flow up. She notes the framework supports 40+ robots across eight categories.

sections.title: Hybrid cloud-edge execution
sections.summary: She explains the architecture under the hood: VLA and policies trained on the cloud using AgentCore, while execution happens on the edge for speed, with Strands deciding which part to call.

sections.title: Future of large VLA models
sections.summary: She argues robot policies/VLA models could scale like large language models, removing the need for fine-tuning. In the meantime, adding an agent is a stepping stone toward that future.

sections.title: 'Do something complex' Telegram demo
sections.summary: She returns to the demo, sends 'do something complex' over Telegram, and Scout invokes the rover_speak tool, announces a 'signature performance,' then turns off its headlights and falls over.

sections.title: Under the hood: model, prompt, data collection
sections.summary: She shows that Strands SDK uses Anthropic Claude Opus 4.8, displays her system prompt defining rules and tool purposes, and explains she can manually navigate Scout to generate training episodes for future datasets.

sections.title: Voice, guardrails, and the 'mirror mirror' Telegram demo
sections.summary: She notes Strands decides which tool to invoke and the voice is OpenAI Realtime, with extra safety guardrails. She then asks Scout over Telegram to spin, analyze the room, and name the best-looking person. Scout spins, scans, and picks Sandy—citing her khaki jeans, sneakers, confident stride, and the blue curtain backdrop.

demonstrations: Type 'turn on your headlights and say hi to everyone' and Scout executes
Scout counts two people via its front camera without being trained to do so
Scout performs a 360-degree spin on command
Send 'do something complex' via Telegram; Scout invokes rover_speak tool and announces a signature performance
Manually navigate Scout to record training episodes for dataset creation
Ask Scout via Telegram to 'spin around, analyze the room, and tell me who is the best-looking person'; Scout scans the room and picks Sandy as 'best looking'
Scout uses OpenAI Realtime voice and a camera analysis to deliver a witty 'mirror mirror' response
limitations: Voice agent had to be disabled because it kept responding to ambient speech on stage
Scout fell over during the demo and required coaxing to stand back up
Headlights turned off unexpectedly after the 'do something complex' command
Scout's 'best-looking person' judgment is biased/always picks the speaker
Currently requires fine-tuning on top of existing VLAs/policies
